summary: I reviewed the dvpwa aiohttp application: the DAO layer (student/course/review/user/mark), views/routes, auth utilities, middlewares, Jinja2 setup, config, and templates/migrations. Overall risk is critical. The app contains an unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create and unauthenticated stored XSS driven by globally disabled Jinja2 autoescaping, compounded by non-HttpOnly session cookies, disabled CSRF protection, unsalted MD5 password hashing, and aiohttp debug mode. Coverage was the full Python source and templates; I did not execute anything (read-only).

findings.title: SQL injection in Student.create via string interpolation
findings.description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement with Python %-formatting of the raw `name` argument directly into the SQL string, instead of passing it as a bound parameter. The `name` value flows from the unauthenticated handler `students` (sqli/views.py:54-57), which reads `data['name']` from a POST to /students/ and passes it straight to Student.create. The POST route has no authorization check in the view (only the template hides the form), so any anonymous client can POST arbitrary `name`. Because psycopg/aiopg execute can run stacked statements, an attacker can break out of the quoted literal (e.g. name = `x'); DROP TABLE students; --`) and read or modify the entire database.
findings.evidence:
q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  # name is attacker-controlled request.post()['name']
await cur.execute(q)  # no parameter binding
Caller: views.students -> await Student.create(conn, data['name']) with no auth gate on POST /students/
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries like the other DAO methods: `await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name})`. Never build SQL by string formatting user input. Additionally enforce server-side authorization on the POST /students/ handler.

findings.title: Stored XSS from globally disabled Jinja2 autoescaping
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so all template variables render unescaped unless an explicit `| e` filter is used. Multiple sinks emit attacker-controlled data without escaping: review text (sqli/templates/course.jinja2:22), course title/description (course.jinja2:14-15), and student name (students.jinja2:16). Review creation (views.review POST) and student creation (views.students POST) are reachable without authentication, so an anonymous attacker can store `<script>` payloads that execute in the browser of any visitor, including the admin who views the course page. Combined with the non-HttpOnly session cookie, this enables session theft and admin takeover.
findings.evidence:
setup_jinja(app, loader=..., context_processors=[...], autoescape=False)
Sink: templates/course.jinja2:22 `{{ review.review_text }}` <- Review.create(course_id, data['review_text']) from unauthenticated POST /courses/{id}/review (views.py:119-129)
findings.recommendation: Set autoescape=True in the aiohttp_jinja2 setup and use the `| safe` filter only where trusted HTML is intentionally rendered. Remove reliance on scattered manual `| e` filters.

findings.title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled
findings.description: The Redis session storage is instantiated with httponly=False, so the session cookie is accessible to client-side JavaScript. Given the stored XSS above, an attacker's injected script can read document.cookie and exfiltrate the session identifier, allowing full hijack of any authenticated user (including the admin) session.
findings.recommendation: Remove httponly=False (the default is True) and additionally set secure=True and an appropriate SameSite attribute for the session cookie.

findings.title: CSRF protection middleware disabled for all state-changing POST routes
findings.description: A working csrf_middleware exists (sqli/middlewares.py:25-38) but is commented out of the middleware chain, so no CSRF validation runs. Although templates emit a `_csrf_token` hidden field, nothing verifies it server-side. State-changing POST endpoints (create student, create course, submit review, evaluate/assign marks, logout) can be triggered cross-site against an authenticated victim, e.g. an attacker can auto-submit a form that assigns marks or creates records as the admin.
findings.evidence:
middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware,
 error_middleware]  # csrf_middleware is commented out; token never validated
findings.recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware list and ensure the token is generated and validated for every non-idempotent request.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5
findings.description: User.check_password compares the stored hash to an unsalted MD5 of the supplied password, and the fixtures store passwords as md5() as well (migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10-13). MD5 is fast and unsalted, so any disclosure of the users table (e.g. via the SQL injection above) allows near-instant offline recovery of credentials via rainbow tables or brute force. Identical passwords also produce identical hashes.
findings.evidence:
return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()
Storage: migrations/001-fixtures.sql -> md5('superadmin'), md5('password') ...
findings.recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hashing function such as bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 (e.g. via passlib), and re-hash stored credentials. Compare using a constant-time verify function.

findings.title: aiohttp application runs with debug mode enabled
findings.description: The Application is constructed with debug=True and error_middleware passes the raw exception object into the error templates. In debug mode aiohttp surfaces additional diagnostic detail, and rendered exception data can leak internal information (paths, query fragments, stack context) to unauthenticated clients who trigger errors. This should not be enabled in production.
findings.evidence:
app = Application(debug=True, middlewares=[...])
error templates receive {'error': exc} (middlewares.py:62-72)
findings.recommendation: Drive debug from configuration and default it to False in production; render generic error pages that do not expose exception internals.
